(p-174)Surah al-Tin (The Fig)

Meccan, though it has been said to be Medinan; its verses number eight.

﴿By the fig and the olive﴾. They are this fig and this olive. Allah, glory be to Him, singled them out from among the fruits to swear by them, because of the noble properties they possess. The fig is a delicious fruit with no equal, a light food that is quickly digested (sari' al-hadm), and a remedy of great benefit: it softens the temperament (yulin al-tab'), dissolves phlegm (yuhallil al-balgham), cleanses the two kidneys, removes the sand (al-raml) that is in the bladder, fattens the body, and opens the blockages (sudad) of the liver and spleen. Abu Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him, related that "a basket of figs was presented to the Prophet ﷺ; he ate of it and said to his companions: 'Eat. If I were to say that a fruit had descended from Paradise, I would say this, for the fruit of Paradise has no pits (ajam). So eat of it, for it cuts off hemorrhoids (al-bawasir) and benefits gout (al-niqris).'" And from Ali ibn Musa al-Rida: "The fig removes bad breath, lengthens the hair, and is a safeguard against paralysis (al-faluj). As for the olive, it is a fruit, a condiment, and a remedy. Even if it had no distinction other than its oil, which has many benefits, while being found in regions where there is no oiliness, that alone would suffice as a virtue." Its tree is the blessed tree referred to in the revelation. Mu'adh ibn Jabal, may Allah be pleased with him, passed by an olive tree, took a twig from it and used it as a siwak (tooth-stick), and said: "I heard the Prophet ﷺ say: 'The olive is an excellent siwak, from the blessed tree; it sweetens the mouth and removes the ḥufra.' And I heard him say: 'It is my siwak and the siwak of the prophets before me.'"

It has been said: they are two mountains of the holy land, called in Syriac Tur Tina and Tur Zayta, because they are the places where the fig and the olive grow. It has also been said: the fig is a mountain between Hulwan and Hamadan, and the olive is the mountains of Syria, since these are their places of growth, as if it were said: "and the places where the fig and the olive grow." Qatada said: the fig is the mountain on which Damascus lies, and the olive is the mountain on which Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) lies. Ikrima and Ibn Zayd said: the fig is Damascus and the olive is Bayt al-Maqdis, and this is the view chosen by al-Tabari. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: the fig is the mosque of the People of the Cave, and the olive is the mosque of Ilya. From Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: the fig is the mosque of Nuh, peace be upon him, which he built on al-Judi, and the olive is the mosque of Bayt al-Maqdis. Al-Dahhak said: the fig is the Sacred Mosque (al-Masjid al-Haram), and the olive is the Farthest Mosque (al-Masjid al-Aqsa). The correct view is the first. Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: it is your fig which you eat and your olive from which you press oil. This is also the view of Mujahid, Ikrima, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, Ata', Jabir, Zayd, Muqatil, and al-Kalbi.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 95, verse 2:

﴿And Mount Sinin﴾ (p-175) It is the mountain upon which Musa (Moses) conversed with his Lord. "Sinin" and "Sayna'" are proper names for the place where it is located, and for this reason the (name) was made an annex to them. "Sinin" is (declined) like "Sinun kabirun" (sound masculine plural) in permissibility of case inflection with waw and ya', retaining the ya' and moving the nun with the case vowels.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 95, verse 3:

﴿And this secure land﴾. That is: the secure one, from amina al-rajulu amanatan, so he is amin (trustworthy). It refers to Makkah, may Allah exalt it. Its trustworthiness (amanah) is that it preserves whoever enters it, just as the amin (trustworthy person) preserves what has been entrusted to him. It is also permissible that it be fa'il (the form fa'il) in the sense of maf'ul (the passive sense), from aminahu, since it is one whose calamities are safe from it (ma'mun al-ghawa'il), just as it is described as al-amin in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿a sanctuary secure﴾, in the sense of dhu amn (possessing security). As for the manner of swearing by these blessed places, filled with the blessings of this world and the religion, it is too evident to need explanation or clarification.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 95, verse 4:

﴿Indeed, We created man﴾, i.e., the species of man, ﴿in the best of forms﴾, i.e., existing in the best state of proportion (taqwim) and balance (ta'dil) in form and meaning. For God Most High brought him into being upright in stature, with well-proportioned limbs, endowed with life, knowledge, power, will, speech, hearing, sight, and other attributes, which are among the examples of the divine attributes and their traces. Some scholars have expressed this by his saying: "Adam was created in His image," and in another narration, "in the image of the Merciful." On this is built the realization of the meaning of his saying: "Whoever knows himself, knows his Lord." He also said: The human soul is immaterial (mujarrad). It is neither inhering in the body nor outside it, but attached to it with the attachment of management (tadbir) and disposal (tasarruf). It uses the body however it wills. When it wills one of the bodily actions, it conveys that to what is in the heart of the animal spirit (al-ruh al-hayawani), which is the most balanced and purest of the spirits, the closest of them to the soul and the most suited to the world of immaterial things, by a spiritual conveyance. It conveys it by means of the spirits in the arteries to the brain, which is the source of the nerves in which lie the powers that move the human being. Then the limbs are moved in whatever suits that act, from its distant and near beginnings, and that act proceeds from it in this manner. So whoever knows his soul in this way, with its attributes and acts, is enabled to ascend to knowledge of the Lord of Might, may His authority be exalted, and to perceive that He, glory be to Him, is exalted above being within the world or outside it. He does in it whatever He wills and decrees whatever He desires, through what He has arranged in it of angels, whose conditions are inferred from what has been mentioned of the spirits and powers arranged in the human world, which is a copy of the greater world and a model of it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 95, verse 5:

As for His saying, ﴿Then We returned him to the lowest of the low﴾, that means: We made him one of the people of the Fire, who are more vile than every vile thing and lower than every low thing, because he did not act in accordance with what requires the attributes with which We created him. Had he acted according to their demands, he would have been in the highest of the high (ʿIlliyyin). It has also been said: "We returned him to the most abject age, which is senility after youth, and weakness after strength," like His saying, ﴿And whomever We grant long life, We reverse him in creation﴾. Whichever is the case, "asfala safilin" is either a circumstantial clause (hal) from the object, meaning: We returned him while he was the lowest of the low; or it is an attribute of an omitted place, meaning: We returned him to a place lowest of the low. The first is more apparent. It has also been read (p-176) "asfala as-safilin" (with the definite article).

The words of His, exalted is He: ﴿Except those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾. According to the first view, it is an exceptive (istithna' muttasil, connected exception) from the pronoun in "radadnahu" (We returned him), since it carries the sense of the plural. According to the second view, it is a disconnected exception (istithna' munqati', disconnected exception), meaning: "But those who were righteous among the decrepit ones." ﴿For them is a reward never to be cut off﴾: not interrupted, in return for their obedience and their patience under God Exalted's trial of old age and decrepitude, and for their bearing of hardships and their performance of worship despite the weakening of their strength; or it means "never to be reckoned as a favour upon them." This sentence, according to the first view, confirms what the exception implies, namely the exclusion of the believers from the rule of being returned, and explains the manner of their condition.

The address in His words, Exalted is He, ﴿So what causes you to deny the Recompense after this?﴾ is to the Messenger (ﷺ). That is: what could make you deny the Recompense, either by way of indication or explicit statement, after these clear proofs that speak to it have become manifest? It was also said: "mā" here means "man" (who). And it was said: the address is to the human being by way of iltifat (a shift from the third person to the second person), to intensify the rebuke and reproach. That is: what makes you a liar concerning the Recompense and its denial after these proofs? The meaning is that the creation of the human being from a drop of semen, his being shaped into a well-proportioned human, and his transformation from state to state, in perfection and in deficiency, are among the clearest proofs of the power of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, over the resurrection and the recompense. So what compels you, O human being, after this decisive proof, to be a liar by denying it?

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 95, verse 8:

﴿Is not Allah the most just of judges?﴾ That is: Is not He who did what has been mentioned the most just of judges in His creating and ordering, so that one might imagine there is no return and no recompense? Since it is impossible that He is not the most just of judges, it is established that there will be a return (i'ada) and a recompense (jaza'). Thus the sentence (al-jumla) is an affirmation (taqrir) of what precedes it. It has also been said that "judgment" (al-hukm) here means "decree" (al-qada'), so the verse is a warning (wa'id) to the disbelievers, and that He will judge them by what they deserve of punishment.

On the authority of the Prophet (ﷺ) that when he recited it, he would say: "Yes, and I am among those who bear witness to that."

Also on his authority (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah al-Tin, Allah the Exalted will grant him the two qualities of well-being (al-'afiya) and certainty (al-yaqin) for as long as he is in the world. And when he dies, Allah the Exalted will grant him a reward equal to the number of those who recited this surah."
